title: Superintelligent judges
author: Chris Wheadon
summary: Chris Wheadon and Daisy Christodoulou of No More Marking test whether large language models can replace human judges in Comparative Judgement assessment of primary writing. They list known LLM-as-judge biases, then test two on 398 decisions across 48 stories by ten-year-olds against a high-reliability set of human judgements. Reversing the order of scripts changed 23 percent of decisions, while human judges show only a tiny left-right bias across tens of millions of decisions. Injecting bogus expert comments made the model abandon 75 percent of its original choices, and text appended to a student's story could flip its verdict with a plausible justification that never mentions the attack. They conclude the models are not superintelligent judges, are open to injection by students, and still need a human in the loop with AI doing the supporting work.
points: LLM judges show position bias, switching nearly a quarter of decisions when script order is reversed, whereas human judges barely do.
Inducement bias is severe, with fake expert tags in the prompt changing 75 percent of decisions and leaving human-model agreement at 15 percent.
Injection attacks embedded in a student's own text can flip an assessment verdict, giving pupils an incentive to game any AI-marked system.
The practical conclusion is not to abandon AI in assessment but to keep a human in the loop and design the human insight and AI support to work together efficiently.
quotes: Judges are asked to choose which is the better piece of writing. Whilst this might seem like a very subjective criterion, extensive research shows that this process delivers much more reliable results than absolute judgements against a mark scheme.

When we changed the order of the scripts, 23% of the decisions changed too. As the model was run with a temperature of zero, that change would seem to be purely due to the reversing of the order of the scripts.
In our database of 37,264,475 human decisions, 19,003,267 chose the left script (51%). A statistically significant, but tiny bias.

You might argue that the LLM is taking into account new evidence and is right to revise its opinion. Perhaps that’s true. But this kind of inducement bias can be triggered not just by a sentence in the prompt, but by a sentence in the student’s writing.

This is obviously a big problem for any large scale use of LLMs for assessment. As soon as students know LLMs are involved in the assessment, there will be an incentive to try injection attacks like this one.
Sadly, so far, the LLMs are not behaving as superintelligent judges. They appear to be easily misled and self-contradictory. For now, we’ll just have to keep on judging.

No. We still feel there are useful ways that LLMs can help teachers, but they cannot operate independently. You need a human in the loop. The big design question is how you can integrate the human insight in a way that is efficient and effective.
